<reason>Both sides were disciplined, kept the motion in view, answered the pressure questions with proper A1:/A2: labels, and avoided fake sourcing. A won the decisive clash. A framed the debate around the counterfactual — what exists the morning after heavy restriction — and never let B off that hook. B's central reply ("if the role exists only because it can be extracted for free, its disappearance is not a social loss") is a coherent normative bite, but A converted it into a live burden: the conversion to paid work is asserted, not shown, and B's own concessions (the person who can take unpaid weeks "already has housing or savings"; the one who cannot "was never walking through" the door) let A land the memorable line that the policy takes from people who don't need help and gives nothing to those who do. B repaired the alleged contradiction reasonably well in [B4.4]-[B4.5] (the door is a filter priced in absorbable unpaid time), and its strongest frame — "leave the unpaid-job label open and every other tool is décor on extraction" — did real work against A's stipend alternative. But A had already given a concrete mechanism (means-tested stipends with duration, supervision and open-advertising conditions attached to scheme access) that B answered only partially, and A's displacement argument — regulation reaches the advertised, open-application post while the family-friend fortnight stays invisible — was met mainly by "informal favours exist either way" rather than by an answer to migration. A also forced a real dilemma on the exemption: credential-gated (excluding the redundant 34-year-old, the refugee lawyer) or vague and retrospective (chilling small charities). B's function test (duration, staff substitution, later credential use) partly answers vagueness but B simply conceded the uncredentialed are out, which cost it. Both sides had one clipped turn, so that execution penalty is roughly symmetrical. A ended with the cleaner comparative rule: certain subtraction versus hypothetical conversion.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's exploitation of B's own concessions in [A4.4]: if the person who can take three unpaid weeks is already cushioned, and the person who cannot "was never walking through the door," then the ban strips opportunity from those who don't need protection and delivers nothing to those who do. B's late naming of a beneficiary ("the applicant who can do three paid weeks and cannot do three unpaid ones") was immediately neutralized by A's point that this beneficiary only exists if the paid weeks appear — the unproven conversion at the heart of PRO's case.</best_rebuttal>
